title: Hamstring Strain Recovery in Sarasota, FL | MD Fit
h1: Hamstring Strain Recovery in Sarasota, FL
description: Pulled hamstring in Sarasota? Dr. Jared Caban on why hamstrings tear, the glute and hip muscles behind it, and how MD Fit rebuilds the back of the thigh.
lead: A hamstring strain is the injury that keeps coming back. The tear heals, you feel fine, you sprint for a pickleball drop shot and it grabs again. Breaking that cycle means fixing why the hamstring was overloaded in the first place.

sections.html:
The sprinting strain is sudden: a sharp grab in the back of the thigh mid-stride, often with a feeling of being shot in the leg, and a limp straight afterward. Bruising may appear a day or two later and drift toward the knee. The stretching strain is slower and higher up, near the sitting bone, after a slide into a split, a high kick, or a yoga session that went too deep. That one aches when you sit and can take longer to settle.

Then there is the chronic version: a tight, nagging ache in the back of the thigh or buttock crease that never had a clear start. It flares with long drives, hills and speed work, and it is frequently not a strain at all but a tight, overworked muscle doing a job the glutes should be doing.

sections.h2: The muscles involved, and why the glutes matter more
sections.html:
• Biceps femoris, the outer hamstring, is the most commonly strained of the three. It refers pain to the back-outside of the knee and up the outer back of the thigh and tightens with sprinting and long sitting.
  • Semitendinosus and semimembranosus, the inner hamstrings, ache at the buttock crease and sitting bone and down to the inner back of the knee. These are the stretching-injury muscles.
  • Gluteus maximus is the root cause in a large share of hamstring strains Dr. Jared sees. When it is weak or slow to fire, the hamstring has to extend the hip and control the knee at the same time, and it fails under speed.
  • Gluteus medius weakness lets the pelvis drop and rotate during running, lengthening one hamstring more than the other with each stride.
  • Adductor magnus works like a fourth hamstring and shares the sitting-bone attachment; it is often tender alongside the strain and contributes to deep inner-thigh ache.

sections.h2: How MD Fit rehabs a hamstring
sections.html: Dr. Jared assesses where the tenderness is, how much strength and length you have compared with the other side, and, critically, whether the glutes are doing their job in a hinge and a single-leg stance. Hands-on release of the hamstring, adductor magnus and glutes reduces guarding and the cord-like tightness that forms along a healing strain. Correction is about the hip hinge: learning to bend at the hips with the glutes leading so the hamstring stops being the only brake. Homework comes from the free MD Fit app, with videos such as Dowel Hip Hinge, Hip Neuroglide and Hip Thrust, progressing to Romanian Deadlift when the tissue is ready. Strengthening finishes with lengthened-position loading and, for athletes, a graded return to running speed, because a hamstring that is strong only in short positions tears again at full stride.

sections.h2: Safe steps for the first days
sections.html:
• Keep walking as normally as pain allows. Complete rest stiffens the muscle and delays recovery; limping teaches a bad pattern.
  • Avoid aggressive stretching early. Pulling on a freshly torn muscle is one of the most common ways to prolong it.
  • Gentle, pain-free movement of the knee and hip several times a day keeps the healing tissue mobile.
  • Sit on a softer surface or shift weight off the sitting bone if the strain is high up.

sections.h2: When the back of the thigh is not the hamstring
sections.html: Pain down the back of the thigh without a clear injury moment is frequently sciatic or referred from the low back, especially if it tingles, changes with coughing, or reaches below the knee. Piriformis and gluteus minimus trigger points send pain down the back of the leg and are regularly mistaken for a chronic hamstring problem. Proximal hamstring tendinopathy sits right at the sitting bone and behaves more like a tendon than a muscle tear. Pain behind the knee with calf swelling is a red flag for a clot, not a strain.

Pickleball is a sport of sudden short sprints from a standing start, which is precisely how hamstrings get hurt, and long sits in the car or at a desk beforehand make it worse. A brief warm-up that includes hip hinges and a few progressively faster strides is the cheapest insurance there is.

timeline: Mild strains often ease within a couple of weeks while more significant tears take several weeks to a few months to return to full-speed sport. High strains near the sitting bone tend to be the slowest. Rushing back before strength at long muscle lengths is restored is the main reason they recur.
redFlags: A loud pop at the sitting bone with a large bruise and difficulty walking: possible complete tendon avulsion, see an orthopedic physician promptly.
Calf swelling, warmth or redness behind the knee or in the calf: a possible blood clot, go to the ER.
Numbness, tingling or weakness in the foot, or foot drop.
Back-of-thigh pain with loss of bladder or bowel control: call 911.
Pain that is worsening after the first week instead of improving.

faq.q: Should I stretch a pulled hamstring?
faq.a: Not aggressively in the early days. Gentle movement is helpful, but hard stretching can re-tear healing fibers. Lengthening comes later through controlled strengthening.

faq.q: Why does my hamstring keep re-tearing?
faq.a: Usually because the glutes are not sharing the load and the hamstring was never strengthened at long lengths before returning to speed. Both are addressed in the MD Fit plan.

faq.q: Can massage help a hamstring strain?
faq.a: Hands-on release helps with guarding and scar tissue once the acute phase has passed. Deep work in the first days is avoided.
When you can walk briskly, hinge and hop without pain and your strength is close to the other side. Speed is added gradually rather than all at once.
